strengths: Compelling and highly practical motivation focusing on semantically lossless MoE serving on unified memory architecture (UMA) edge devices to avoid security and alignment degradation from quantization.

Innovative compression-scheduling co-design that splits BF16 parameters into low-entropy exponent chunks (E-chunks) and high-entropy sign-mantissa chunks (SM-chunks), effectively overlapping CPU decompression with storage I/O.
Rigorous theoretical foundation, including a provable (3 - 1/L)-approximation ratio on the scheduling makespan and a maximum entropy proof for the dynamic programming-based cache-planning algorithm.

Significant performance improvements (up to 72.77% latency reduction and up to 6.76x higher throughput) over strong baselines like MoE-Infinity and DeepSpeed across multiple models and hardware configurations.
weaknesses: Evaluations are limited to NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin platforms. Testing on more heterogeneous or constrained consumer hardware (e.g., mobile SoC platforms with UFS/eMMC storage, Raspberry Pi) would strengthen the generalizability claims of the proposed on-device serving system.

The system's pipeline assumes a high-speed SSD read rate (3.5 GB/s). On standard mobile devices with lower storage bandwidth, the optimal balance between I/O and CPU decompression might shift, potentially affecting the tightness of the schedule overlap.

While the focus is on lossless serving, providing a baseline comparison or discussion with a state-of-the-art quantized serving framework (e.g., EdgeMoE) on the Pareto frontier of memory vs. speed would provide a clearer practical perspective on when to prefer ZipMoE.

The potential impact of continuous CPU multi-threaded decompression on battery consumption, thermal throttling, and overall resource contention with the OS in real-world mobile settings is not thoroughly explored.

strengths: Compelling and highly practical motivation: serving large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models on-device without lossy quantization to avoid security vulnerabilities and semantic degradation.

Clever co-design of lossless compression and systems scheduling: the paper exploits the low entropy of the exponent bits in BF16 format, separating them from the high-entropy sign/mantissa bits to allow parallelized decompression that is entirely hidden behind the I/O of incompressible parts.

Strong theoretical backing: the authors provide a scheduling algorithm with a provable approximation bound (within 3 - 1/L of the optimal makespan) and formulate a maximum entropy cache pool planning framework resolved using dynamic programming.

Thorough evaluation on representative edge platforms (Jetson AGX Orin) with popular real-world MoE models, demonstrating remarkable improvements of up to 72.77% latency reduction and 6.76x throughput over SOTA baselines (MoE-Infinity, DeepSpeed, Accelerate).
weaknesses: The evaluation is restricted to the Jetson AGX Orin platform. Testing on other mainstream UMA-based edge platforms (e.g., Apple Silicon or mobile phones with Snapdragon SoCs) would strengthen the generalizability claims.

While the paper analyzes resource contention on memory bandwidth (showing it is negligible), it lacks a thorough evaluation of CPU worker thread interference under multi-tenant environments where other background tasks compete for CPU cycles.

Algorithm 4 relies on a grid search to find the optimal memory ratios. Although acceptable for a few cache pools, a discussion of the computational complexity and scalability of this grid search for larger models and more complex hierarchies is missing.

strengths: Compelling and highly practical motivation: the paper targets the serving of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models on resource-constrained edge devices with Unified Memory Architecture (UMA), addressing a key bottleneck (I/O storage latency) without compromising model accuracy via lossy quantization.

Innovative hardware-software co-design: by separating weight parameters into highly compressible exponent bits and incompressible sign-mantissa bits, the system elegantly overlaps CPU-parallel lossless decompression with SSD read operations.

Strong theoretical foundation: the proposed cache-affinity scheduler comes with a provable constant-factor approximation guarantee (Theorem 3.1), and the cache-planning framework is mathematically grounded in maximum entropy and dynamic programming.

Thorough and convincing empirical evaluation: the authors implemented a complete prototype and tested it on real-world hardware (NVIDIA Jetson) using diverse open-source MoE models. The results demonstrate massive speedups and throughput improvements over state-of-the-art baselines like MoE-Infinity and DeepSpeed.
weaknesses: Platform specificity: the design is heavily tailored to Unified Memory Architectures (UMA) where CPU and GPU share physical RAM. The benefits might not fully translate to edge devices with discrete memory pools or architectures with very weak CPU performance.

Overhead of runtime scheduling: the proposed scheduler dynamically constructs DAGs and manages hierarchical cache pools at runtime. While the authors state this overhead is small, a more detailed breakdown of the CPU-side scheduling overhead per token would be valuable.

Assumption of deterministic execution times: the scheduling and makespan estimation rely on profiled execution times ($p_n$) for experts. In real-world multi-tenant scenarios, dynamic hardware contention could lead to performance variations that deviate from the static scheduling model.

strengths: Innovative system design that exploits the low-entropy characteristic of BF16 exponent bits to implement a lossless compression-decompression pipeline, preserving exact model behavior without any accuracy degradation.

Solid theoretical foundation, including a cache-affinity scheduler with a provable approximation ratio of (3 - 1/L) for the makespan, and a rank-based cache planning algorithm proven to achieve maximum entropy.
Comprehensive system-level implementation and optimizations (e.g., zero-copy memory access on unified memory architecture, vectorized GPU kernel for fast parameter reconstruction).

Thorough evaluation on representative edge platforms (Jetson AGX Orin) across various MoE models (DeepSeek, Qwen, Switch) demonstrating massive performance improvements over strong state-of-the-art offloading baselines like MoE-Infinity and DeepSpeed.
weaknesses: The experimental evaluation is restricted to the NVIDIA Jetson platform with a Unified Memory Architecture (UMA). The applicability and performance of the proposed methods on platforms with separated CPU-GPU memory (non-UMA) or resource-constrained mobile phones remain unverified empirically.

The parallel decompression pipeline relies on the availability of multiple idle CPU cores (e.g., 3 or more worker threads). On mobile or edge devices with highly volatile co-located background tasks, this assumption might lead to performance degradation or resource contention.

While lossless compression preserves exact model behavior, the size reduction (68%-74% of the original size) is inherently limited compared to lossy quantization methods (which achieve 4x or more reduction). A more detailed discussion on the performance/memory trade-off between ZipMoE and state-of-the-art quantized MoE serving systems would be valuable.

strengths: Compelling motivation focusing on lossless compression for MoE serving, which preserves exact model behavior and avoids security and accuracy vulnerabilities associated with lossy quantization.
Excellent hardware-software co-design tailored specifically to the Unified Memory Architecture (UMA) of mobile SoCs, shifting MoE execution from I/O-bound to parallel compute-bound.
Strong theoretical backing with a provable approximation guarantee (Theorem 3.1) for the cache-affinity scheduler's makespan and a maximum-entropy proof (Theorem 3.2) for the cache pool planning.

Comprehensive and convincing evaluation on diverse MoE architectures (DeepSeekV2-Lite, Qwen1.5-MoE, SwitchTransformers) on actual Jetson hardware, demonstrating massive improvements in TPOT and TTFT compared to state-of-the-art baselines.
weaknesses: The evaluation is restricted to a single platform type (NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin). While Jetson is a representative edge device, testing on other popular UMA platforms such as Apple Silicon (M-series) or Raspberry Pi would strengthen the generalizability claims.

The design specifically targets the BF16 format by decomposing it into sign-mantissa and exponent bits. It is unclear how easily this technique can extend to other emerging floating-point formats such as FP8 (e.g., E4M3 or E5M2) or NF4, which are increasingly relevant for on-device inference.

While the cache planning algorithm is executed offline/at startup, the runtime scheduling overhead of dynamically constructing DAGs and running Algorithm 1 at each layer step during decoding is not quantified. Clarifying this runtime overhead in milliseconds would help confirm its absolute cost is negligible.

strengths: Practical and well-motivated design: The paper successfully identifies and addresses the mismatch between traditional offloading paradigms and edge/mobile SoC hardware architectures (Unified Memory Architecture, shared bus, multi-core CPUs). It effectively shifts the MoE serving bottleneck from storage I/O to parallel CPU-centric decompression.

Solid theoretical foundation: The proposed cache-affinity scheduler is backed by a provable $(3 - 1/L)$-approximation bound on the makespan, and the hierarchical cache planning is proved to achieve maximum entropy (Bayes robust) under observed expert popularity ranks.

Fine-grained, compression-aware cache management: Transitioning from binary caching (fully cached or not) to a multi-tiered cache hierarchy (full tensors, compressed tensors, sign-mantissa chunks, and exponent chunks) allows the system to achieve up to 2x tensor coverage under tight memory budgets.

Rigorous and comprehensive evaluation: ZipMoE is compared against strong, widely used baselines (MoE-Infinity, DeepSpeed, Accelerate, and FineMoE) across three distinct MoE architectures. The paper includes highly detailed ablation studies, sensitivity analyses under distribution shifts, and experiments isolating the impact of the OS page cache.
weaknesses: Limitation in evaluation hardware: The evaluation is conducted solely on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin boards (64GB and 32GB). While Jetson is a prominent edge platform, actual mobile devices (such as Android/iOS smartphones or Raspberry Pi) represent a major share of 'on-device' deployments. Validating the system on these platforms would strengthen the claims of mobile generalizability.

Impact of CPU thermal throttling and multi-tenant resource contention: On actual consumer mobile devices, the OS heavily regulates the CPU to manage thermal output and battery life. Additionally, other concurrent user applications may compete for CPU resources. Since ZipMoE relies on active multi-threaded CPU decompression, further discussion or evaluation of the system under restricted/throttled CPU conditions would be highly beneficial.

Real-world interactive latency: While ZipMoE achieves massive speedups compared to other lossless offloading baselines, the absolute performance under tight memory budgets (e.g., Time-Per-Output-Token of ~0.4–0.5s) remains somewhat slow for real-time interactive chat on edge devices. Discussing how the lossless compression pipeline could be combined with model quantization to further bridge this gap would increase the practical impact of the work.
